title: Weight decay is ridge
objectives: Show that weight decay is the ridge penalty, and choose its strength on validation loss.

screens.title: A curve through every point
screens.prose: A 1-64-64-1 tanh net is fitted to 30 noisy points of $\sin 3x$ (`default_rng(0)`, noise sd 0.3) by 2,000 Adam steps. With no penalty it bends through nearly every point. The slider adds $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ to the loss.
screens.question: As $\lambda$ rises from 0, what does the validation error do?

options.text: It falls, then rises again once the fit is too stiff
It keeps falling: the larger the penalty, the better
options.why: At $\lambda = 0.1$ the fit is much flatter and the error is back up to 0.26.

options.text: It rises from the start, since the fit gets worse on the 30 points
options.why: The training fit gets worse, but the validation error first falls, to 0.10.

options.text: It barely changes: the penalty only shrinks weights
options.why: It moves from 0.17 to 0.10 and back up to 0.26.

hints.text: Watch the curve and the caption together.
Small penalties smooth the wiggles; large ones flatten everything.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the caption at each stop.

byKey.down: That is the trap of more is better: past the bottom of the U the fit underfits.

explain.text: The penalty trades fit for smoothness. Validation error falls from 0.17 to 0.10, then rises as the curve flattens: the U from ridge regression.

screens.title: Why it is called decay
screens.prose: Name it: adding $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ to the loss adds $\lambda\mathbf{w}$ to the gradient, so an SGD step is $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow (1 - \eta\lambda)\mathbf{w} - \eta\mathbf{g}$: every weight shrinks by a factor before the usual step. That is **weight decay**; for a linear model it is exactly ridge.
screens.question: With $\eta = 0.1$ and $\lambda = 0.01$, what is the factor $1 - \eta\lambda$?

feedback.correct: $1 - 0.1 \times 0.01 = 0.999$: each step keeps 99.9% of every weight, then adds the gradient step.

byKey.lam: You used $1 - \lambda$; the step size multiplies it.
byKey.prod: That is $\eta\lambda$ itself, the share removed.

explain.text: The gradient of $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ is $\lambda\mathbf{w}$, so one step removes $\eta\lambda = 0.001$ of every weight. With no data gradient, 1,000 such steps leave $0.999^{1000} \approx 0.37$ of it.

screens.title: One decayed step
screens.prose: A weight $w = 2$ has data gradient $g = 0.5$. Take one SGD step with $\eta = 0.1$ and $\lambda = 0.01$.
screens.question: What is the new $w$? Give 3 decimal places.

byKey.nodecay: That is the plain step; the decay removes another 0.002.
byKey.full: You added $\lambda$ to the gradient instead of $\lambda w$.

explain.text: The penalty adds $\lambda w = 0.02$ to the gradient, so the step is $0.1 \times 0.52 = 0.052$ and $w = 1.948$. Writing it as decay or as a penalty gives the same number for SGD.

screens.title: Choosing lambda
screens.prose: Each bar is the validation error after training with one penalty. As in `stat-learning` l7, we choose $\lambda$ on the validation points, never on the test points.

state.caption: 200 validation points; the noise alone gives about 0.09.

screens.question: Which $\lambda$ would you choose?

hints.text: The two are close; 0.01 is lower.

feedback.correct: 0.01, at 0.10, just below 0.001 at 0.11. A gap that small is within the noise of 200 points: either is a sound choice.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the lowest validation bar.

byKey.zero: No penalty fits the noise: the highest error but one.
byKey.big: At 0.1 the fit is too stiff and underfits.

explain.text: 0.01 is lowest, at 0.10. With 200 validation points the two best bars differ by less than their noise, so the flat bottom of the U, not one value, is the finding.

screens.title: Adam and the penalty
screens.prose: With Adam, a penalty in the loss and decay applied directly differ. Adam divides the whole gradient, penalty included, by $\sqrt{\hat v}$, so large-gradient weights get less decay. **AdamW** (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) applies the decay outside: $w \leftarrow w - \eta\big(\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon) + \lambda w\big)$.
screens.question: At step 1, $w = 1$, $g = 0.2$, $\eta = 0.01$, $\lambda = 0.1$. What is AdamW's new $w$? Give 3 decimal places.

hints.text: Adam's first step is $\eta$ times the sign of the gradient: 0.01.

feedback.correct: $1 - 0.01(1 + 0.1) = 0.989$. With the penalty in the loss, the gradient $0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3$ is rescaled to a step of 0.01, so $w = 0.990$: the decay vanished.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply Adam's step, then the decay.

byKey.l2: That is the penalty in the loss: Adam rescales it away at step 1.
byKey.sgd: That is an SGD step on the penalised loss.

explain.text: In the loss, the penalty is divided by $\sqrt{\hat v}$ along with the data gradient, so at step 1 it changes nothing: 0.990. AdamW keeps it separate, giving 0.989.

screens.title: Tuned on the test set
screens.prose: Dee tries six penalties and reports the one with the lowest error on the test set, then quotes that test error as how well the net will do.
screens.question: What is wrong?

options.text: The test set chose $\lambda$, so its error is optimistic
Nothing: the test set is held out from training
options.why: It was held out from the weights, but not from the choice of $\lambda$.

options.text: She should penalise the biases too
options.why: Biases are usually left unpenalised; a bias sets a level, not a wiggle.

options.text: Six values are too few to choose from
options.why: More values make the test error look even better by luck.

hints.text: Which data set made the choice?
A set used to choose cannot also grade the choice.
Validation chooses; the test set is read once (`validation` l1).

feedback.correct: The choice used the test set, so the reported error is optimistic; as in `stat-learning` l7, tune on validation and read the test set once.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the test set was used for.

byKey.fine: That is the trap: any data used to pick a setting stops being a test of that setting.

explain.text: Picking the best of six on the test set fits the test noise a little, like any fitting. Choose on validation and report the test error once, at the end.

widget.how: Submit runs 7 hidden tests, compared to $10^{-9}$: two decayed steps, the two Adam updates at steps 1 and 4 (they must differ), five decayed steps in a row, and two choices from recorded losses.

mutants.symptom: Shrinks by 1 - lam, leaving out the step size.
Treats AdamW as Adam with the penalty in the gradient.
Decays by lam, not lr * lam.

hints.text: Shrink by `1 - lr * lam`, then step.
Write one plain Adam step as a helper and call it twice.

feedback.correct: All pass: at step 1 the two Adam updates give 0.990 and 0.989.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test in the results.

screens.title: Ten thousand weights, two thousand days
screens.prose: A return-prediction net has 10,000 weights and 2,000 days of data: plenty of room to memorise. The penalty is the first lever, chosen on a walk-forward validation block (`validation` L2). Take $\eta = 0.01$ and $\lambda = 0.01$.
screens.question: With no data gradient, what share of a weight survives 1,000 steps of decay? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: $0.9999^{1000} = 0.9048$, close to $e^{-0.1}$: a weight the data stops supporting fades by about a tenth.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by the factor once per step.

byKey.lin: You subtracted 1,000 times 0.0001; the factor compounds.
byKey.lam: You used a factor of 0.99, leaving out the step size.

explain.text: $(1 - \eta\lambda)^{1000} = 0.9048$. Weights that the data keeps pushing survive; weights only noise supports decay away.

ideas: A penalty $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ adds $\lambda\mathbf{w}$ to the gradient, so SGD multiplies every weight by $1 - \eta\lambda$ each step: weight decay, which is ridge for a linear model.
Choose $\lambda$ on validation data: here the error falls from 0.17 to 0.10 and climbs back to 0.26 as the fit stiffens; at $\lambda = 1$ the net is a constant.
Adam rescales a penalty in the loss, so it differs from decay; AdamW applies the decay outside the rescaling.
summary.trap: Tuning the penalty on the test set spends the test set: choose on validation, test once.

quiz.prose: SGD with weight decay uses $\eta = 0.05$ and $\lambda = 0.002$.
quiz.question: What factor multiplies every weight each step? Give 4 decimal places.

explain.text: $\eta\lambda = 0.0001$, so each step keeps 0.9999 of every weight.

quiz.prose: At $\lambda = 1$ the net gives the same prediction at every $x$, and its validation error is 0.5702; the validation targets have variance 0.5183.
quiz.question: What has the net become?

options.text: A constant, the same answer for every input
A perfect fit, since every prediction agrees
options.why: An error near the targets' variance is what a constant scores.
An overfit net has a low training error; this one is high on both.

options.text: A straight line through the data
options.why: A sloped line would give different predictions at different $x$.

feedback.correct: A constant: every weight was crushed to 0, leaving only the output bias.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What does one prediction for every $x$ mean?

explain.text: A constant at the training mean scores about the variance of the targets (0.5183) plus the gap between the two means: 0.5702. Too large a penalty is the edge case: the net predicts a constant.

quiz.question: For a linear model $\hat y = \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{w}$, what is SGD with weight decay $\lambda$ minimising?

options.text: The squared error plus $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$: ridge regression
The squared error plus $\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert_1$: the lasso
options.why: The decay term $\lambda\mathbf{w}$ comes from a squared penalty, not an absolute one.

options.text: Plain least squares; decay only speeds it up
options.why: Decay changes the minimum: it shrinks the weights.

options.text: Nothing in closed form: it is a heuristic
options.why: For SGD, decay is exactly the gradient of a squared penalty.

feedback.correct: Ridge: the gradient of $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2$ is the decay term $\lambda\mathbf{w}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which penalty has gradient $\lambda\mathbf{w}$?

explain.text: $\nabla\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \lambda\mathbf{w}$, so decayed SGD descends the ridge objective.
